title: A Swayamvara That Was Never Meant to Be
story:
The king of Kundina had agreed to a swayamvara he did not want. Bhishmaka had let his son Rukmi send out the invitations — every throne in the land summoned to choose a husband for the princess Rukmini — and now the kings were arriving by every road: chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry pouring into the city until the streets seemed to dance with armed men. And the more the kings assembled, the more Bhishmaka felt the whole affair slipping out of his hands.

He had come to Krishna with his trouble, seeking him out as a man seeks the one person who might set a disaster right. "My son, out of his childish nature, wishes to give away his sister in a swayamvara," he said. "I do not like it. I wish my daughter to choose the one person she sees and no other. Forgive my son's bad conduct, O Lord; be propitiated."

Krishna's answer was not gentle. "If your son is this arrogant while still a boy, how arrogant will he be when he grows old?" he said. "A king who speaks a falsehood, even before a single king, consumes himself with the fire of Yama's tortures. Truthfulness is the foremost religious duty of kings; Brahma himself pointed it out in the days of yore. So how can your son now utter a lie before all these kings assembled in your city?" And then his voice sharpened further. "You say you know nothing of this great gathering — yet kings like the sun and moon sit at your tables, and cars, elephants, horses, and infantry have made a wild dance through Kundina. How can you not know of your son's work? Perhaps you thought my arrival was not conducive to your well-being, and so you offered no hospitality to one you deemed unworthy. Manu and the law-givers have ordained that he who puts obstacles in the way of a maiden wastes himself in hell. That is why I did not enter your assembly hall, nor accept your welcome. Kaishika, ever fond of guests, gave rest to my followers; and I, with Garuda beside me, live here as in the city of the gods."

Bhishmaka bowed low under the force of those words. "Be propitiated, O Lord of the celestial region," he said. "Forgive me, lord of the land of mortals. I am possessed by the darkness of ignorance; give me eyes of wisdom. We are men of perverse understanding with fleshy eyes. But now we have obtained you, who are the God of gods. Having obtained your shelter, I entertain no fear."

Then Krishna softened, and what he said next changed everything. "O king, the goddess-like form of Rukmini has brought me to this place," he said. "I will not tell you to give her to me and to no one else. But listen to what the gods decreed long ago. When they assembled on the summit of Mount Sumeru, in the days of yore, they said to her: 'Go with your husband to the world of men. Having been born in the house of Bhishmaka in the city of Kundina, be united with Keshava.' I tell you this plainly, king; do whatever you think proper after due consideration."

"But know this," he went on. "Truly, your daughter Rukmini is not a woman. She is the goddess Lakshmi herself, born among mortals at the words of Brahma. She must not be given away in a swayamvara where all the kings will be assembled. Invite one bridegroom, and confer her on him with proper rites — that is a Kshatriya's duty. You cannot give Lakshmi away in a swayamvara." He paused, and when he spoke again there was something almost like a smile in his voice. "To put impediments in the way of that swayamvara, Garuda, son of Vinata, has been sent here by the king of the gods. And I too have come — to witness the festival of the kings, and to see your daughter, the beautiful lotus among women."

Bhishmaka heard it all in silence: that his daughter was not his to give at all, that the gods had decided her fate on a mountain before she was born, that the ceremony his son had announced across the land could never bind her. He had come to Krishna fearing a disaster; he left knowing that what he had feared was the will of the gods themselves.
reflection: The revelation reframes the entire swayamvara: Rukmini is not a prize to be contested but a goddess whose destiny was fixed before her birth, and so no assembly of kings can undo it. Krishna's sternness with Bhishmaka — about falsehood, hospitality, and the law — clears the ground for the gentle truth he then delivers.
next_story_tease: Before he left Kundina, Krishna would show Bhishmaka what he truly was.
hero_scene: Krishna, facing King Bhishmaka in the quiet of Kundina, one hand raised as he speaks the revelation — that Rukmini is the goddess Lakshmi, born to be united with Keshava — while Garuda waits behind him in the fading light.
visual_elements: the assembled kings glimpsed through the doorway
